fetched_contents.text: Factors influencing full immunization coverage among 12–23 months of age children in Ethiopia: evidence from the national demographic and health survey in 2011 Abstract Background Immunization remains one of the most important public health interventions to reduce child morbidity and mortality. The 2011 national demographic and health survey (DHS) indicated low full immunization coverage among children aged 12–23 months in Ethiopia. Factors contributing to the low coverage of immunization have been poorly understood. The aim of this study was to identify factors associated with full immunization coverage among children aged 12–23 months in Ethiopia. Methods This study used the 2011 Ethiopian demographic and health survey data. The survey was cross sectional by design and used a multistage cluster sampling procedure. A total of 1,927 mothers with children of 12–23 months of age were extracted from the children’s dataset. Mothers’ self-reported data and observations of vaccination cards were used to determine vaccine coverage. An adjusted odds ratio (AOR) with 95 % confidence intervals (CI) was used to outline the independent predictors. Results The prevalence of fully immunized children was 24.3 %. Specific vaccination coverage for three doses of DPT, three doses of polio, measles and BCG were 36.5 %, 44.3 %, 55.7 % and 66.3 %, respectively. The multivariable analysis showed that sources of information from vaccination card [AOR 95 % CI; 7.7 (5.95-10.06)], received postnatal check-up within two months after birth [AOR 95 % CI; 1.8 (1.28-2.56)], women’s awareness of community conversation program [AOR 95 % CI; 1.9 (1.44-2.49)] and women in the rich wealth index [AOR 95 % CI; 1.4 (1.06-1.94)] were the predictors of full immunization coverage. Women from Afar [AOR 95 % CI; 0.07 (0.01-0.68)], Amhara [AOR 95 % CI; 0.33 (0.13-0.81)], Oromiya [AOR 95 % CI; 0.15 (0.06-0.37)], Somali [AOR 95 % CI; 0.15 (0.04-0.55)] and Southern Nation and Nationalities People administrative regions [AOR 95 % CI; 0.35 (0.14-0.87)] were less likely to fully vaccinate their children. Conclusion The overall full immunization coverage in Ethiopia was considerably low as compared to the national target set (66 %). Health service use and access to information on maternal and child health were found to predict full immunization coverage. Appropriate strategies should be devised to enhance health information and accessibility for full immunization coverage by addressing the variations among regions. Background Immunization is one of the key interventions to achieving the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), especially the goal to reduce deaths among children under five years old [1]. Childhood vaccinations have been shown to be effective in protecting children against vaccine preventable diseases in low and middle income countries [2, 3]. Vaccines prevent more than 2.5 million child deaths per year [1]. The Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) was initiated by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1974 to control vaccine preventable diseases worldwide [4]. In Ethiopia, EPI was first launched in 1980 and its vaccination schedule is based on the WHO recommendations [5, 6]. The national guideline was later published in 1988 and recently the Ethiopian immunization policy was updated in 2007 [7]. Tremendous progress in improving vaccination coverage has been made over the past four decades in many Africa countries [5]. Ethiopia has made encouraging improvements in accessibility and provision of primary healthcare services, especially since the establishment of the Health Extension Program in 2003. Recently, the country is also deploying and reinforcing the Women’s Development Army (WDA) initiative under the package of the health extension program. Immunization is a key component of the health extension program package. However, full vaccination coverage has not been completed in Ethiopia as planned. The full immunization coverage remained only 24.3 % in 2011 [8, 9] and as a result many children in Ethiopia have not received the benefits of full immunization [10]. The country has slightly higher infant and under 5 mortality rates that account for 59 and 88 deaths per 1000 live births, respectively [8] as compared to other developing countries [11]. Barriers for full vaccination coverage in other settings have been described and includes: lower parental education [12–14], lower income [13–15], being female gender of the child [16, 17], traditional and Muslim religions [18, 19], place of delivery and mothers received a postnatal check-up after 2 months of birth [20], household assets and expenditure, ethnicity, age and parity [21] were documented in Asian and African countries. In Ethiopia, malnutrition, vaccine preventable diseases and malaria were identified as the major causes of death among the under 5 children [22]. Furthermore, mothers’ knowledge about child immunization, postponing child immunization and perceived health institution support [23], institutional delivery and antenatal care (ANC) attendance [24], tetanus toxoid vaccine, place of residence and household visited by health workers [25], women’s decision making autonomy, number of under-five children in the household, mother’s education and proximity to health facilities [26] were factors identified through small scale studies in the country. Though there have been few studies done fragmentally in different parts of Ethiopia, the social determinants of low vaccination coverage and non-uptake of immunization services have been poorly understood at the national level. fetched_contents.text: Immunization coverage of 12–23 months old children and associated factors in Jigjiga District, Somali National Regional State, Ethiopia Abstract Background Immunization coverage in Ethiopia is less than the herd immunity level desired to prevent the spread of eight target diseases targeted by the World Health Organization’s Expanded Program of Immunization. In particular, the Somali region of the country still has by far the lowest level of immunization coverage. The objective of this study was to measure the immunization coverage of 12–23 months old children and associated factors in the urban and rural areas of Jigjiga district. Methods A community based cross-sectional survey was conducted in 582 households with 12–23 months old children in two urban and four rural wards. The data were collected from mothers or caregivers through interviews based on pre-tested and structured questionnaires and from the review of vaccination cards. Data were processed using SPSS version 16. To identify factors associated with the immunization status of children, bivariate and multiple logistic regression analyses were worked out and the Hoshmer and Lemeshow’s goodness-of-fit was used to assess the fitness of multiple logistic regression model. Results Three–fourth (74.6%) of the children surveyed were ever vaccinated, whereas 36.6% were fully vaccinated. The immunization coverage rate from card assessment for Bacillus Calmette-Guérin was 41.8%, while for Oral Polio Vaccine Zero, Oral Polio Vaccine One /Pentavalent1, Oral Polio Vaccine Two /Pentavalent2, Oral Polio Vaccine Three /Pentavalent3, and measles were 10.4%, 41.1%, 33.9%, 27.5%, and 24.9%, respectively. Maternal literacy (AOR = 3.06, 95% CI = 1.64, 5.71), Tetanus Toxoid Vaccine (AOR = 2.43, 95% CI = 1.56, 3.77), place of delivery (AOR = 2.02, 95% CI = 1.24, 3.28), place of residence (AOR = 2.04, 95% CI = 1.33, 3.13), and household visits by health workers (AOR = 1.92, 95% CI = 1.17, 3.16), were found to be factors significantly associated with full immunization in the multivariate logistic regression analysis. Conclusions The overall immunization coverage was found to be low. Hence, to increase the immunization coverage and reduce the incidences of missed opportunity, delivery in the health institution should be promoted, the outreach activities of the health institutions should be strengthened and greater utilization of health services by mothers should be encouraged. fetched_contents.text: Effective coverage of child immunisation service in Ethiopia Abstract Vaccines are one of the safest and most cost-effective interventions to prevent disease and disabilities worldwide. Yet, nearly 19 million children do not receive basic vaccines and most of them are from low and middle-income countries. The Sustainable Development Goal 3 aims at eliminating preventable deaths of newborns and under-five children by 2030. However, Ethiopia has a high child mortality rate, and most of them are from preventable causes. Quality provision of immunisation could reduce vaccine-preventable morbidity and mortality. Despite this, the quality-adjusted coverage of immunisation services in Ethiopia has not been well-documented. We used the Kids’ record from the 2019 Ethiopian Demographic and Survey (EDHS) and the health facility recode from the 2021–2022 Ethiopian Service Provision Assessment (ESPA). The EDHS and ESPA data were linked using administrative boundary linkage using administrative regions and city administrations. The crude coverage was weighted before linking with the ESPA dataset. Health facilities which provide child immunisation services were included. The quality of immunisation service provision was constructed from 14 indicators. The quality of immunisation was calculated as the sum of the availability of items in each domain, divided by the total number of items in the domain, and finally multiplied by 100. The effective coverage was measured as the product of contact coverage and quality of immunisation service provision. We use STATA 17 for analysis. A total of 951 respondents who have a live children aged 12–23 month were included. The national effective coverage of immunisation was 34.3% (95% Confidence interval (CI): 33.0, 35.5) with a large variation in different regions, ranged from 14.8% in Afar to 83.5% in Addis Ababa. The crude coverage of immunisation services was 39.6% (95% CI: 36.5, 42.7), ranged from 19.2% in Afar to 87.39% in Addis Ababa. The overall score for quality of immunisation service was 82% (95% CI: 80.44, 83.51). The quality ranged from 74.6% in SNNPR to 95.5% in Addis Ababa. The quality of immunisation varies with the managing authority of health facilities, private facilities had the highest quality (90% (95% CI: 85.35, 95.36)) and government facilities scored the lowest quality (82% (95% CI: 80.06, 83.22)). There was low effective coverage of immunisation services provision in Ethiopia. The effective coverage was lower in the pastoral regions (Afar and Somali). Government facilities and facilities in rural areas had lower-quality immunisation services. Facilities in SNNPR and Afar region had low-quality of immunisation service. Policymakers should focus on improving the quality of government facilities and the facilities in rural areas and pastoral regions to improve immunisation services. Synthesis of the main sociodemographic determinants of immunization coverage

The evidence consistently identifies several sociodemographic factors that are associated with immunization coverage among Ethiopian children aged 12–23 months. The strongest and most recurrent associations are wealth, maternal education, residence, and access to health services. Across the provided sources, higher wealth and better maternal education are generally linked to higher immunization coverage, while certain disadvantaged groups and rural/remote settings are associated with lower coverage [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R4][N4-R1].

### Which factors are most consistently associated with higher or lower coverage?
The most consistently associated positive factors are:
- **Maternal education**: Higher maternal education is strongly linked to better immunization outcomes. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that as maternal education increases, the completion of childhood vaccination accelerates [N4-R1]. In the Ethiopia-specific study, maternal literacy was associated with full immunization, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.06 (95% CI 1.64–5.71) [N2-F2].
- **Wealth**: Higher household wealth is consistently associated with better immunization coverage. A low-income country systematic review found that children in middle and richer wealth quintile households were 43–57% more likely to have full immunization coverage than children in poorer quintiles [N3-R4]. The Ethiopia-specific study also found that women in the rich wealth index were more likely to fully vaccinate their children [N1-F1].
- **Place of residence**: Urban residence is often associated with better coverage than rural residence. In the Ethiopia study, place of residence was a significant predictor of full immunization, with an odds ratio of 2.04 (95% CI 1.33–3.13) [N2-F2]. The broader systematic review also notes that geographic access can affect vaccine impact and vaccination dropout [N3-R2].
- **Access to health services**: Receipt of postnatal check-up within two months after birth, visits by health workers, and institutional delivery are consistently associated with higher coverage. In the Ethiopia study, postnatal check-up within two months after birth was linked to full immunization, with an odds ratio of 1.8 (95% CI 1.28–2.56) [N1-F1], and household visits by health workers were also associated with full immunization [N2-F2].

The most consistently associated negative factors are:
- **Poverty or disadvantaged wealth quintiles**: Lower coverage is more common among poorer households. The systematic review noted that inequalities in wealth, education, and geographic access can affect vaccine impact and vaccination dropout [N3-R2]. In Ethiopia, the rich wealth index was associated with higher coverage, while the evidence base also implies lower coverage in poorer households [N1-F1][N3-R4].
- **Certain regional and ethnic differences**: Ethiopia-specific evidence shows that some regions and ethnic groups are less likely to fully vaccinate children. In the 2011 EDHS study, women from Afar, Amhara, Oromiya, Somali, and Southern Nations Nationalities and Peoples regions were less likely to fully vaccinate their children, with odds ratios ranging from 0.07 to 0.35 [N1-F1].
- **Rural/remote residence and poor access**: Rural and pastoral regions, such as Afar and Somali, have historically lower coverage and poorer quality immunization service provision [N5-F3]. The broader systematic review also notes that geographic access can affect vaccine impact and vaccination dropout [N3-R2].

### How wealth, education, and residence interact with coverage outcomes
Wealth, education, and residence interact in a layered way. Wealthier households are more likely to have higher coverage, but education is an even stronger and more consistent predictor in the evidence. In Ethiopia, maternal literacy was strongly associated with full immunization, and the rich wealth index was also associated with higher coverage [N2-F2][N1-F1]. At the same time, residence matters: urban residence is generally associated with better coverage than rural residence, and rural and pastoral regions tend to have both lower coverage and lower-quality service provision [N2-F2][N5-F3]. This suggests that residence is a proxy for broader access constraints, including distance to health facilities, availability of health workers, and community-level health infrastructure.

### Whether maternal characteristics and antenatal care matter across studies
Maternal characteristics do matter across studies. Maternal education, literacy, and knowledge are repeatedly associated with better immunization outcomes. In the Ethiopia study, maternal literacy was a strong predictor of full immunization, and the systematic review and meta-analysis found that higher maternal education accelerates childhood vaccination completion [N4-R1][N2-F2]. Antenatal care also matters, but the evidence is more mixed in the provided sources. The Ethiopia study found that received postnatal check-up within two months after birth was associated with full immunization [N1-F1], while the broader systematic review highlights antenatal care visits as a determinant of measles vaccination coverage [N3-R1]. However, the provided evidence does not establish a single uniform pathway for antenatal care across all vaccines or settings. In other words, antenatal care appears relevant, but the evidence here is strongest for postnatal check-up and maternal knowledge rather than a single universal antenatal-care effect.

Overall, the sociodemographic determinants in the evidence are consistent in direction: education and wealth are positive predictors, whereas poverty, rural residence, and disadvantaged regions are negative predictors. The strongest consistent factors are maternal education and household wealth, with residence and access to health services acting as important mediating influences [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-R4][N4-R1].

Evaluate interventions and policy options to address disparities

The evidence supports a combination of health system and community-level interventions to close immunization coverage gaps. The most likely interventions are those that improve access, quality of service, and health worker outreach, while community-based approaches can help overcome barriers such as distance, low awareness, and mistrust. Ethiopia-specific evidence suggests that these interventions should be targeted at rural and pastoral areas, where coverage is lowest and service quality is also lower [N2-F2][N5-F3][N6-R2].

### Which interventions are most likely to close coverage gaps?
The interventions most likely to close coverage gaps are:
- **Mobile health clinics and outreach activities**: Mobile clinics are explicitly described as effective tools for reducing health disparities by delivering interventions to difficult-to-reach populations [N6-R2]. In Ethiopia, mobile health clinics can increase access to vaccinations and reduce missed opportunities, especially in rural and underserved areas [N6-R2][N6-R3].
- **Strengthening health facility services and quality of care**: Improving the quality of immunization services is a major priority. The Ethiopia study found that quality of immunization service provision was an important determinant of effective coverage, with lower quality in government facilities and rural areas [N5-F3]. The same source also emphasizes that interventions such as training health extension workers, expanding primary healthcare services, and implementing an integrated health extension package can improve immunization coverage [N5-F3].
- **Increasing household visits by health workers**: The Ethiopia study found that household visits by health workers were associated with full immunization [N2-F2]. This suggests that community engagement and home-based outreach can improve coverage.
- **Promoting institutional delivery and postnatal care**: Postnatal check-up within two months after birth was associated with full immunization in Ethiopia [N1-F1]. This implies that improving maternal and child health services before and after birth can support immunization uptake.

### How health system and community-level approaches compare
Health system approaches are stronger for improving the delivery of vaccines and service quality. Ethiopia-specific evidence points to health facility-based improvements, including better vaccine availability, trained staff, and facility readiness, as critical for increasing effective coverage [N5-F3]. Mobile clinics and outreach are community-level approaches that can reach populations outside formal facilities and help close gaps in rural and pastoral areas [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence here suggests a complementary rather than exclusive relationship: health system strengthening creates the infrastructure for coverage, while community outreach ensures that coverage reaches populations with limited access.

### What Ethiopia-specific evidence supports or limits adoption
Ethiopia-specific evidence strongly supports the adoption of mobile clinics and health worker outreach, as well as facility-based quality improvements. The study from Jigjiga District found that maternal literacy, Tetanus Toxoid Vaccine receipt, place of delivery, place of residence, and household visits by health workers were all associated with full immunization, and it recommended promoting institutional delivery, strengthening outreach, and encouraging greater health service use [N2-F2]. The effective coverage study also found that effective coverage was lower in government facilities, rural areas, and pastoral regions, supporting targeted interventions in those settings [N5-F3].

The evidence also limits some generalizations. First, the Ethiopia-specific studies are based on cross-sectional survey data rather than randomized trials, so causality cannot be definitively established [N2-F2][N5-F3]. Second, the evidence highlights variation by region and residence, implying that interventions must be tailored to local contexts rather than applied uniformly [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Finally, the evidence shows that coverage remains uneven across Ethiopia, with Addis Ababa having much higher coverage than Afar and Somali [N5-F3], which supports focused attention on low-coverage regions rather than a one-size-fits-all solution.

In conclusion, the most promising interventions are mobile clinics, outreach by health workers, and facility-based quality improvements, with Ethiopia-specific support for these approaches in rural, pastoral, and low-coverage areas [N6-R2][N5-F3][N2-F2]. The evidence supports a dual emphasis on strengthening the health system and expanding community-based access, but it also warns that interventions must be adapted to local service delivery constraints and regional disparities [N5-F3][N2-F2].

Assess the Ethiopia-specific context and coverage measurement environment

Ethiopia’s immunization measurement and reporting environment is anchored in the Demographic and Health Surveys (EDHS), with additional health facility and service provision assessment data used to improve coverage estimates. The evidence shows that coverage is measured through a combination of self-reported vaccination status, vaccination cards, and facility records, and that effective coverage combines contact coverage with service quality [N5-F3][N7-R2][N7-R3].

### How immunization is measured and reported in Ethiopia
In Ethiopia, immunization coverage is measured using multiple data sources:
- **Demographic and Health Survey (DHS)**: The EDHS is the main national survey used to measure coverage. The 2011 EDHS found 24.3% full immunization coverage among children aged 12–23 months, and later surveys showed increasing coverage over time [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5].
- **Vaccination cards and maternal reports**: Coverage is assessed by mothers’ self-reported data and observations of vaccination cards. The 2011 study explicitly used vaccination cards to determine vaccine coverage [N1-F1].
- **Health facility records**: The 2016 EDHS included a health facility component that recorded data on children’s vaccinations, which were then combined with other data sources [N5-R4]. More recent work links the Kids’ record from the 2019 EDHS with the health facility recode from the 2021–2022 Ethiopian Service Provision Assessment (ESPA) [N5-F3].
- **Effective coverage**: A recent Ethiopia-specific study introduced effective coverage as the product of contact coverage and quality of immunization service provision [N5-F3]. This means coverage is not only measured by whether a child receives a vaccine, but also by whether the service is delivered effectively.

### Key program barriers and service-delivery constraints
The evidence identifies several barriers and constraints that shape immunization delivery in Ethiopia:
- **Low coverage and uneven distribution**: Ethiopia has historically had low coverage, with the 2011 EDHS reporting 24.3% full immunization coverage, and later surveys showing coverage rose to 39% in 2016 and 44% in 2019, but still uneven across regions [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F3].
- **Quality of service provision**: The 2021–2022 ESPA-linked analysis found that the national effective coverage of immunisation services was 34.3%, with large regional variation and lower coverage in pastoral regions such as Afar and Somali [N5-F3]. Quality of service was also lower in government facilities and rural areas [N5-F3].
- **Access and missed opportunities**: The Ethiopia study emphasizes that delivery in the health institution should be promoted and outreach activities strengthened to reduce missed opportunities [N2-F2]. This suggests that even when services exist, families may miss immunization opportunities due to distance, poor awareness, or poor service delivery.
- **Facility readiness and health worker availability**: The effective coverage study found that vaccine availability, trained staff, and facility readiness are important for service quality [N5-F3]. It also found that government facilities had lower quality than private facilities, which may reflect resource constraints and staffing issues [N5-F3].
- **Regional and rural disparities**: Ethiopia-specific evidence shows that coverage varies greatly across regions, with Addis Ababa having much higher coverage than Afar and Somali [N5-F3]. The 2016 EDHS also found that coverage varied greatly across geographical regions [N2-R3].

### How regional and urban/rural differences shape coverage
Regional and urban/rural differences strongly shape coverage in Ethiopia. The evidence consistently shows:
- **Urban advantage**: Urban residence is associated with better coverage than rural residence [N2-F2]. In Ethiopia, Addis Ababa had the highest effective coverage at 83% in 2019, while Afar and Somali had much lower coverage [N5-F3].
- **Rural disadvantage**: Rural areas and pastoral regions have lower coverage and lower-quality immunization services [N5-F3][N2-F2]. The Ethiopia study found that place of residence was a significant predictor of full immunization [N2-F2].
- **Regional variation**: Coverage varies greatly across Ethiopian regions. The 2016 EDHS reported that 39% of children aged 12–23 months were vaccinated, with rates varying greatly across regions [N2-R3]. The recent effective coverage study found coverage ranged from 14.8% in Afar to 83.5% in Addis Ababa [N5-F3].
- **Pastoral regions**: Afar and Somali have especially low coverage and low service quality [N5-F3]. The 2011 EDHS also showed that some regions were less likely to fully vaccinate children [N1-F1].

Overall, Ethiopia’s coverage measurement environment is robust but still constrained by regional and rural disparities. Coverage is measured through DHS, vaccination cards, and facility records, with effective coverage incorporating service quality [N5-F3][N7-R2][N7-R3]. The main barriers include low coverage, uneven regional distribution, poor service quality in government and rural facilities, and missed opportunities due to access constraints and low facility readiness [N5-F3][N2-F2].

### 3) Do maternal characteristics and antenatal care matter across studies?

Maternal characteristics matter across studies. Maternal education, literacy, and knowledge are repeatedly associated with better immunization outcomes [N4-R1][N2-F2].
